claim: Kinesin-5 motor proteins perform essential mitotic functions by providing the force that separates the spindle poles apart during spindle assembly, maintenance, and elongation.
source: Kinesin-5 motor proteins perform essential mitotic functions by providing the force that separates the spindle poles apart during spindle assembly, maintenance, and elongation reviewed in Goulet and Moores, 2013; Kapoor, 2017; Mann and Wadsworth, 2019; Scholey et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2018; Waitzman and Rice, 2014.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Kinesin-5 motors are homotetramers, with two pairs of catalytic domains located on opposite sides of a central minifilament.
source: These motors are homotetramers, with two pairs of catalytic domains located on opposite sides of a central minifilament (Acar et al., 2013; Gordon and Roof, 1999; Kashina et al., 1996; Scholey et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The unique structure of kinesin-5 motors enables them to crosslink the antiparallel microtubules of the spindle and to slide them apart by moving in the plus-end direction of the two MTs that they crosslink.
source: This unique structure enables kinesin-5 motors to crosslink the antiparallel microtubules (MTs) of the spindle and to slide them apart by moving in the plus-end direction of the two MTs that they crosslink (Kapitein et al., 2005; Shapira et al., 2017; Shimamoto et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: Plus-end directed motility of kinesin-5 motors is essential to separate the spindle poles.
source: Because of the MT architecture within the mitotic spindles, plus-end directed motility of kinesin-5 motors is essential to separate the spindle poles (Goulet and Moores, 2013; Mann and Wadsworth, 2019; Singh et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: It was previously believed that N-terminal kinesin motors are exclusively plus-end directed.
source: Moreover, since the catalytic domains of kinesin-5 motors are located at their N-termini, it was previously believed that such N-terminal motors are exclusively plus-end directed.
evidence: The claim describes a historical belief in the field.

claim: Three kinesin-5 motors – Saccharomyces cerevisiae Cin8 and Kip1 and Schizosaccharomyces pombe Cut7 – move processively toward the minus-end of the MTs and switch directionality under different experimental conditions.
source: Recently, however, several studies have demonstrated independently in single-molecule motility assays that three kinesin-5 motors – the Saccharomyces cerevisiae Cin8 and Kip1 and the Schizosaccharomyces pombe Cut7 – move processively toward the minus-end of the MTs and switch directionality under different experimental conditions (Britto et al., 2016; Düselder et al., 2015; Edamatsu, 2014; Fallesen et al., 2017; Fridman et al., 2013; Gerson-Gurwitz et al., 2011; Roostalu et al., 2011; Shapira and Gheber, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: The molecular mechanism and physiological implications of bi-directional motility of kinesin-5 motors remain elusive.
source: The above-described body of work notwithstanding, the molecular mechanism and physiological implications of such bi-directional motility remain elusive.
evidence: The claim describes the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The majority of kinesin motors share a mechanical structural element of 10–18 amino acids, termed the neck linker (NL), which connects the two catalytic domains of the kinesin dimers.
source: The majority of kinesin motors share a mechanical structural element of 10–18 amino acids, termed the neck linker (NL), which connects the two catalytic domains of the kinesin dimers, enabling them to step on the same MT.
evidence: The claim describes a structural feature common to kinesin motors based on established knowledge.

claim: For N-terminal plus-end directed kinesins, the NL is located at the C-terminal end of the catalytic domain, between the last helix of the catalytic domain (α6) and the neck helix (α7) that is required for dimerization.
source: For N-terminal plus-end directed kinesins, the NL is located at the C-terminal end of the catalytic domain, between the last helix of the catalytic domain (α6) and the neck helix (α7) that is required for dimerization (Kozielski et al., 1997; Vale and Fletterick, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: During 'hand-over-hand' stepping in the plus-end direction, the NL isomerizes between a disordered 'undocked' conformation in the presence of ADP and an ordered, motor-domain-bound 'docked' conformation in the presence of ATP.
source: It has been proposed that during 'hand-over-hand' stepping in the plus-end direction, the NL isomerizes between a disordered 'undocked' conformation in the presence of ADP and an ordered, motor-domain-bound 'docked' conformation in the presence of ATP, with the docked conformation pointing toward the plus-end of the MT (Gigant et al., 2013; Goulet et al., 2014; Rice et al., 1999; Rosenfeld et al., 2001; Tomishige et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The docked conformation of the NL is stabilized by N-terminal sequences upstream of the motor domain, termed the cover strand (CS), which form a β-sheet with the first half of the docked NL, termed β9.
source: It is believed that the docked conformation is stabilized by N-terminal sequences upstream of the motor domain, termed the cover strand (CS), which form a β-sheet with the first half of the docked NL, termed β9 (Geng et al., 2014; Goulet et al., 2012; Hwang et al., 2008; Khalil et al., 2008; von Loeffelholz et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies.

claim: An asparagine residue in the middle of the NL is predicted to serve as a latch (N-latch), holding the docked NL along the core motor domain, which is conserved in processive plus-end directed kinesins.
source: Additional stabilization of the docked NL conformation is provided by an asparagine residue in the middle of the NL that is predicted to serve as a latch (N-latch), holding the docked NL along the core motor domain, which is conserved in processive plus-end directed kinesins (Hwang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The docked NL is also stabilized by an interaction between amino acids in the second half of the NL, termed β10, and amino acids in β7 and the loop 10 of the motor domain.
source: The docked NL is also stabilized by an interaction between amino acids in the second half of the NL, termed β10, and amino acids in β7 and the loop 10 of the motor domain (Hwang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The isomerization of the NL between the docked and undocked conformations is believed to be a force-generating transition in kinesin motors.
source: The importance of the isomerization of the NL between the docked and undocked conformations – as a force-generating transition in kinesin motors (Cao et al., 2014; Clancy et al., 2011; Gigant et al., 2013; Goulet et al., 2014; Shang et al., 2014) – is believed to lie in its role in coordinating nucleotide binding and hydrolysis (Clancy et al., 2011) and regulating motor velocity, processivity, and force production (Budaitis et al., 2019; Düselder et al., 2012; Higuchi and Endow, 2002; Hughes et al., 2012; Muretta et al., 2015; Muretta et al., 2018; Schief and Howard, 2001; Shastry and Hancock, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: The transition to, and stabilization of, the docked NL conformation bring the trailing head forward in the plus-end direction and are critical for plus-end directed motility.
source: During plus-end directed stepping of pairs of motor domains connected via the NL, the transition to, and stabilization of, the docked NL conformation bring the trailing head forward in the plus-end direction and are thus critical for plus-end directed motility.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the described mechanism of NL docking.

claim: The dynamics of the NL isomerization in bi-directional kinesins has to allow stepping in both directions.
source: Since bi-directional kinesin motors can move in both plus- and minus-end directions on the MTs, the dynamics of the NL isomerization in these kinesins has to allow stepping in both directions.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the bi-directional motility of these motors.

claim: The role of the NL in regulating the motor functions of bi-directional kinesins has not been reported prior to this study.
source: Thus far, however, the role of the NL in regulating the motor functions of bi-directional kinesins has not been reported.
evidence: The claim describes the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Cin8 variants that were partially active exhibited a smaller number of stabilizing H-bonds between the docked NL and motor domain, compared to wild type Cin8.
source: We showed that, among these variants, those that were partially active exhibited a smaller number of stabilizing H-bonds between the docked NL and motor domain, vs. wild type (wt) Cin8.
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling data presented in the manuscript (Figure 3 and Table 2).

claim: Elimination of a conserved backbone H-bond between a glycine in the N-latch position of Cin8 resulted in a non-functional variant.
source: In addition, we showed that elimination of a conserved backbone H-bond between a glycine in the N-latch position of Cin8 resulted in a non-functional variant, indicating that stabilization of this H-bond is critical for the functionality of Cin8.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing non-viability of the Cin8NLCut7-NG variant (Figure 1C).

claim: Partial replacement of the NL of Cin8 with homologous sequences from the NLs of plus-end directed kinesins resulted in the generation of non-functional Cin8 variants that could neither move in the minus-end direction nor crosslink MTs in vitro.
source: Partial replacement of the NL of Cin8 with homologous sequences from the NLs of plus-end directed kinesins resulted in the generation of non-functional Cin8 variants that could neither move in the minus-end direction nor crosslink MTs in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing defects in motility and MT crosslinking (Figures 4 and 5).

claim: In the Cin8NLEg5 variant containing sequences from the NL of the plus-end directed vertebrate kinesin-5 Eg5, the number of stabilizing H-bonds between the N-latch asparagine and the motor domain was larger than that in wt Cin8.
source: In one such variant, containing sequences from the NL of the plus-end directed vertebrate kinesin-5 Eg5, the number of stabilizing H-bonds between the N-latch asparagine and the motor domain was larger than that in wt Cin8, indicating that additional stabilization of the N-latch position is incompatible with the functionality of Cin8.
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling data presented in Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: A single replacement of the conserved N-latch asparagine with glycine in the Cin8NLEg5 variant decreased the number of N-latch stabilizing H-bonds and rescued the majority of the defects of the non-functional variant, both in vivo and in vitro.
source: In this variant, a single replacement of the conserved N-latch asparagine with glycine, as originally present in Cin8, decreased the number of N-latch stabilizing H-bonds and rescued the majority of the defects of the non-functional variant, both in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing partial rescue of function in the Cin8NLEg5-NG variant (Figures 1, 2, 4-6).

claim: Exact H-bond stabilization that allows a certain degree of flexibility in NL docking is critical for the functionality of the bi-directional kinesin-5 Cin8.
source: Thus, we propose that exact H-bond stabilization that allows a certain degree of flexibility in NL docking is critical for the functionality of the bi-directional kinesin-5 Cin8.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental and modeling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cin8 variants containing NL sequences from plus-end directed kinesin motors are not functional in cells.
source: Cin8 variants containing partial NL sequences from exclusively plus-end directed kinesin motors (Cin8NLKHC and Cin8NLEg5) failed to grow at all the examined temperatures (Figure 1C), thereby indicating that these variants were not functional in cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cells deleted for Cin8 (but with functional Kip1) and expressing the Cin8NLEg5 variant exhibited significantly longer doubling times than cells expressing wt Cin8.
source: In addition, cells deleted for Cin8 (but with functional Kip1) and expressing the Cin8NLEg5 variant exhibited significantly longer doubling times than cells expressing wt Cin8 (Table 1), as is consistent with the impaired functionality of this variant.
evidence: The claim is supported by doubling time data presented in Table 1.

claim: Cells expressing the Cin8NLCut7 variant were viable at 23°C and 26°C, but not at temperatures above 30°C.
source: Importantly, cells expressing the Cin8 variant with the NL sequence of the bi-directional Cut7 (Cin8NLCut7) were viable at 23°C and 26°C, but not at temperatures above 30°C (Figure 1C), thereby indicating that at least some of the Cin8 functions are preserved in the Cin8 variant containing the NL sequence from a different bi-directional kinesin.
evidence: The claim is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The doubling time of cells expressing the Cin8NLCut7 variant was significantly longer than that of cells expressing wt Cin8 in both the presence and absence of Kip1.
source: The doubling time of cells expressing the Cin8NLCut7 variant was significantly longer than that of cells expressing wt Cin8 in both the presence and absence of Kip1 (Table 1), which is consistent with the partial functionality of this variant.
evidence: The claim is supported by doubling time data presented in Table 1.

claim: Cin8NLEg5 and Cin8NLCut7 variants accumulated with monopolar spindles in cells with functional Kip1.
source: Moreover, in cells with functional Kip1, variants containing the NL sequence from the plus-end directed Eg5 and bi-directional Cut7 accumulated with monopolar spindles (Figure 2A, B), indicating that both variants were defective in the spindle assembly function in S. cerevisiae cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by spindle length distribution data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Cin8NLEg5 exhibited diffusive localization in the nucleus, in contrast to wt Cin8 and Cin8NLCut7 which concentrated near the SPBs.
source: Prior to bipolar spindle formation, when the two SPBs had not yet separated, wt Cin8 and Cin8NLCut7 concentrated near the SPBs, at the minus-ends of nuclear MTs (Figure 2C–E). This localization pattern is consistent with the minus-end directed motility of these variants on the nuclear MTs (Figure 2D; Shapira et al., 2016). In contrast, Cin8NLEg5 exhibited diffusive localization in the nucleus (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by localization data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: Cin8NLEg5 occupied a significantly larger area than wt Cin8 and Cin8NLCut7 in cells with pre-assembled spindles.
source: Quantitative analysis in cells with pre-assembled spindles did indeed indicate that Cin8NLEg5 occupied a significantly larger area than wt Cin8 and Cin8NLCut7 (see Materials and methods) (Figure 2E), indicating that localization of this variant is significantly more diffusive in the nucleus, probably due to reduced affinity to nuclear MTs.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative localization data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The minus-end directed motility is impaired in the Cin8NLEg5 variant, although it is maintained in the partially functional Cin8NLCut7.
source: In addition to the diffusive nuclear localization and in contrast to wt Cin8 and Cin8NLCut7, Cin8NLEg5 also exhibited residual attachment to the nuclear MTs (Figure 2C, white arrow). Such localization, similar to the previously reported pattern of the tailless Cin8 mutant that had lost its minus-end directionality preference (Düselder et al., 2015; Shapira et al., 2016) suggests that the minus-end directed motility is impaired in the Cin8NLEg5 variant, although it is maintained in the partially functional Cin8NLCut7.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from localization data shown in Figure 2C and comparison to previously published data.

claim: The Cin8-G522N variant exhibited reduced viability at 35°C and 37°C when expressed as the sole source of kinesin-5.
source: We found that the variant in which this glycine had been replaced with asparagine, namely, Cin8-G522N, exhibited reduced viability at 35°C and 37°C, when expressed as the sole source of kinesin-5 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: cin8Δ kip1Δ cells expressing the Cin8-G522N variant exhibited longer doubling times than cells expressing wt Cin8.
source: Consistently, cin8Δ kip1Δ cells expressing the Cin8-G522N variant exhibited longer doubling times than cells expressing wt Cin8 (Table 1), thereby indicating that the functionality of Cin8 was undermined by the replacement of glycine at position 522 with asparagine.
evidence: The claim is supported by doubling time data presented in Table 1.

claim: Reinstating the original glycine at position 522 in the Cin8NLEg5 variant (Cin8NLEg5-NG) rescued the non-viable phenotype, supporting the viability of cin8Δ kip1Δ cells at temperatures up to 30℃.
source: Strikingly, reinstating the original glycine rescued the non-viable phenotype of the Cin8NLEg5 variant, supporting the viability of cin8Δ kip1Δ cells at temperatures up to 30℃ (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The doubling time of cin8Δ kip1Δ cells expressing Cin8NLEg5-NG was longer than that of cells expressing wt Cin8.
source: The doubling time of cin8Δ kip1Δ cells expressing Cin8NLEg5-NG was longer than that of cells expressing wt Cin8 (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by doubling time data presented in Table 1.

claim: No accumulation of monopolar spindles was observed in cells expressing the Cin8NLEg5-NG variant in the presence of Kip1, in contrast to cells expressing Cin8NLEg5.
source: However, in the presence of Kip1, and in contrast to cells expressing Cin8NLEg5, no accumulation of monopolar spindles was observed in cells expressing the Cin8NLEg5-NG variant (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by spindle length distribution data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The Cin8NLEg5-NG variant localized near the SPBs, at the minus-end of the nuclear MTs, similarly to the localization pattern of wt Cin8.
source: Finally, prior to spindle assembly, the Cin8NLEg5-NG variant localized near the SPBs, at the minus-end of the nuclear MTs, similarly to the localization pattern of wt Cin8 (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by localization data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: Minus-end directed motility is restored in the Cin8NLEg5-NG variant, which moves in the minus-end direction on nuclear MTs and concentrates at the SPBs.
source: This pattern suggests that, in contrast to Cin8NLEg5, minus-end directed motility is restored in the Cin8NLEg5-NG variant, which moves in the minus-end direction on nuclear MTs and concentrates at the SPBs (Shapira et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from localization data shown in Figure 2C-E and comparison to published data.

claim: Cells expressing the Cin8NLCut7-NG variant were not viable at all the examined temperatures.
source: Surprisingly, we found that whereas cells expressing the Cin8NLCut7 variant were partially viable at 23°C and 26°C, cells expressing the variant in which the N-latch asparagine had been replaced by glycine (termed Cin8NLCut7-NG) were not viable at all the examined temperatures (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cells expressing the Cin8NLCut7-NG variant accumulated with monopolar spindles.
source: Consistently, cells expressing the Cin8NLCut7-NG variant accumulated with monopolar spindles (Figure 2A), indicating that this variant is defective in the spindle assembly function.
evidence: The claim is supported by spindle length distribution data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The Cin8NLCut7-NG variant exhibited diffusive localization in higher percent of cells with monopolar spindles, compared to wt Cin8.
source: Finally, the Cin8NLCut7-NG variant exhibited diffusive localization in higher percent of cells with monopolar spindles, compared to wt Cin8 (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by localization data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: β9 of the NLs of all Cin8 variants forms two H-bonds with the non-motor N-terminal residues, L73 and I75.
source: Indeed, our modeling revealed that β9 of the NLs of all our Cin8 variants forms two H-bonds with the non-motor N-terminal residues, L73 and I75 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, red dashed lines), supporting the notion that the N-terminal CS of Cin8 stabilizes the docked conformation of the NL.
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: wt Cin8 forms a conserved backbone H-bond between G157 in a loop between α1 and β3 and the N-latch G522 in the NL.
source: According to our models, wt Cin8 forms a conserved backbone H-bond between G157 in a loop between α1 and β3 and the N-latch G522 in the NL (Hwang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling data shown in Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: wt Cin8 forms two H-bonds between F412 in β7 and S523 and F524 in the NL and an additional H-bond between S523 and F524 of the NL.
source: In addition, wt Cin8 forms two H-bonds between F412 in β7 and S523 and F524 in the NL and an additional H-bond between S523 and F524 of the NL (Figure 3 and Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling data shown in Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: The array of H-bonds in wt Cin8 was not recapitulated in any of the examined variants.
source: This array of H-bonds was not recapitulated in any of the variants we examined, which might explain why none of these variants is able to exhibit the full function of Cin8 in cells (Figures 1 and 2 and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of modeling data (Figure 3 and Table 2) with experimental data (Figures 1 and 2 and Table 1).

claim: The non-functional Cin8NLEg5 variant forms a highly stabilized H-bond array involving the N-latch asparagine (N522) of the NL.
source: Interestingly, the non-functional Cin8NLEg5 variant also forms only one H-bond between F412 in β7 and K524 in the NL. However, according to our models, it forms a highly stabilized H-bond array involving the N-latch asparagine (N522) of the NL, which replaces the G522 of Cin8.
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling data shown in Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: In Cin8NLEg5, two H-bonds are formed between the amide nitrogen of N522, one with G157 and the other with I414 in β7.
source: In Cin8NLEg5, similarly to wt Cin8, a conserved backbone H-bond is formed between G157 and N522. In addition, two H-bonds are formed between the amide nitrogen of N255, one with G157 and the other with I414 in β7 (Figure 3 and Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling data shown in Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: The extra stabilization of the NL during docking, provided by H-bonds of the amide group of N522, is one of the reasons for lack of functionality of Cin8NLEg5 in cells.
source: Since the Cin8NLEg5-NG variant is partially functional in cells, while Cin8NLEg5 is not (Figures 1 and 2 and Table 1), we propose that the extra stabilization of the NL during docking, provided by H-bonds of the amide group of N522, is one of the reasons for lack of functionality of Cin8NLEg5 in cells.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on comparison of modeling data (Figure 3 and Table 2) with experimental data (Figures 1 and 2 and Table 1).

claim: The non-functional Cin8NLCut7-NG is unable to form the highly conserved H-bond between G157 and G522.
source: Finally, the non-functional Cin8NLCut7-NG forms only one H-bond between F412 in β7 and L524 of the NL and is unable to form the highly conserved H-bond between G157 and G522 (Figure 3 and Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling data shown in Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: All the NL variants exhibited significantly lower levels of MT-bound motors than wt Cin8.
source: We found that all the NL variants exhibited significantly lower levels of MT-bound motors than wt Cin8 (Figure 4A), thereby indicating that the NL affects the MT-affinity of Cin8.
evidence: The claim is supported by MT-binding assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The majority of Cin8NLEg5 and Cin8NLCut7-NG variants exhibited no motor motility at 140 mM KCl.
source: Moreover, we also found that the majority of Cin8NLEg5 and Cin8NLCut7-NG variants, which were unable to support yeast cell viability as a sole source for kinesin-5, exhibited no motor motility at 140 mM KCl (not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by motility assay data mentioned in the text.

claim: Cin8NLEg5 exhibited only bi-directional diffusive motility, with no minus-end directed bias, at lower salt concentration.
source: We found that under these conditions, Cin8NLEg5 exhibited only bi-directional diffusive motility, with no minus-end directed bias, in contrast to wt Cin8, which exhibited processive minus-end directed motility (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Under high ionic strength conditions, all Cin8 NL variants moved processively in the minus-end direction of the MTs.
source: We found that under these conditions, consistent with previous reports (Gerson-Gurwitz et al., 2011; Shapira et al., 2016; Shapira et al., 2017), all Cin8 NL variants moved processively in the minus-end direction of the MTs (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Single molecules of wt Cin8 exhibited fast processive movements towards the minus ends of MTs, with a high average velocity of −318±4 nm/s under high ionic strength conditions.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Gerson-Gurwitz et al., 2011; Roostalu et al., 2011; Shapira and Gheber, 2016; Shapira et al., 2017), we found that under high ionic strength conditions, single molecules of wt Cin8 exhibited fast processive movements towards the minus ends of MTs, with a high average velocity of −318±4 nm/s (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Mutating asparagine at position 522 to glycine (Cin8NLEg5-NG) dramatically changed the motile behavior, inducing processive minus-end directed motility.
source: Remarkably, in contrast to the diffusive motility of the Cin8 variant containing the NL sequence of the plus-end directed Eg5 (Cin8NLEg5) (Figure 4B, orange arrows), mutating asparagine at position 522 to glycine (Cin8NLEg5-NG) dramatically changed the motile behavior, inducing processive minus-end directed motility (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: The average velocity of the Cin8NLEg5-NG variant was lower than that of wt Cin8.
source: Although the average velocity of the Cin8NLEg5-NG variant was lower than that of wt Cin8 (Figure 4D), the processive minus-end directed motility of this variant under the high ionic strength conditions indicates that glycine at position 522 in the NL modulates the minus-end directed motility of Cin8.
evidence: The claim is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Mutation of glycine at position 522 to asparagine in wt Cin8 resulted in slower minus-end directed motility, compared with that of the original wt Cin8.
source: Consistently, in wt Cin8, mutation of glycine in this position to asparagine resulted in slower minus-end directed motility, compared with that of the original wt Cin8 (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Cin8NLCut7 exhibited processive minus-end directed motility, but with reduced velocity compared with that of wt Cin8.
source: Furthermore, Cin8NLCut7, the Cin8 variant with the NL sequence of the bi-directional Cut7 containing asparagine at position 522 (Figure 1C), also exhibited processive minus-end directed motility, but with reduced velocity compared with that of wt Cin8 (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The average run length of the motile Cin8NLCut7 was significantly shorter than that of wt Cin8.
source: We found that the average run length of the motile Cin8NLCut7 was significantly shorter than that of wt Cin8.
evidence: The claim is supported by run length data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cin8 induced the accumulation of MT bundles, thereby increasing the apparent fluorescence intensity of these bundles compared with that of single MTs.
source: Consistent with previous reports (Gheber et al., 1999), we found that Cin8 induced the accumulation of MT bundles, thereby increasing the apparent fluorescence intensity of these bundles compared with that of single MTs (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by MT-bundling assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The MT-bundling activity of wt Cin8 was concentration dependent, inducing MT bundling at a minimal molar ratio of ~1:40 Cin8 motors to tubulin dimer.
source: The MT-bundling activity of wt Cin8 was concentration dependent, inducing MT bundling at a minimal molar ratio of ~1:40 Cin8 motors to tubulin dimer (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by MT-bundling assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: With the exception of Cin8NLEg5, all NL variants induced MT bundling in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: With the exception of Cin8NLEg5, all NL variants (Figure 1C) induced MT bundling in a concentration-dependent manner, with the fluorescence intensity of bundles induced by high concentrations of motors being significantly higher than that of MTs without the addition of motors (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by MT-bundling assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: At high motor protein concentrations, the functional NL variants, Cin8-G522N, Cin8NLCut7 and Cin8NLEg5-NG, induced MT bundling to a significantly greater extent compared with the non-functional Cin8NLEg5.
source: Moreover, at high motor protein concentrations, the functional NL variants, Cin8-G522N, Cin8NLCut7 and Cin8NLEg5-NG, induced MT bundling to a significantly greater extent compared with the non-functional Cin8NLEg5.
evidence: The claim is supported by MT-bundling assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The MT-bundling activity of the NL variants is strongly correlated with the ability of these variants to support cell viability as a sole source of kinesin-5.
source: This finding indicates that the MT-bundling activity of the NL variants is strongly correlated with the ability of these variants to support cell viability as a sole source of kinesin-5 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of MT-bundling data (Figure 5D) with viability data (Figure 1C).

claim: All the functional NL variants exhibited reduced ability to bundle MTs, compared with wt Cin8.
source: However, all the functional NL variants exhibited reduced ability to bundle MTs, compared with wt Cin8, a finding that is consistent with the reduced affinity for MTs of these variants (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by MT-bundling assay data shown in Figure 5D and MT-binding data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A single change of the asparagine at position 522 of Cin8NLEg5 to glycine produced a variant that induced MT bundling at high protein concentrations.
source: Finally, in contrast to the Cin8NLEg5 variant, which failed to induce MT bundling, a single change of the asparagine at position 522 of Cin8NLEg5 to glycine, produced a variant that induced MT bundling at high protein concentrations (Figure 5D), thereby indicating that glycine at position 522 is important for the MT-crosslinking and bundling activity of Cin8.
evidence: The claim is supported by MT-bundling assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In the presence of 125 mM KCl and ~3 ng/ml wt Cin8, MT sliding was observed, and in more than 50% of cases, this sliding was plus-end directed.
source: Consistently with previous results (Shapira et al., 2017), we found that in the presence of 125 mM KCl and ~3 ng/ml wt Cin8, MT sliding was observed. In more than 50% of cases, this sliding was plus-end directed, with the minus-end of the moving MT leading (Figure 6 and Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by MT sliding assay data shown in Figure 6.

claim: MT capturing or sliding was not observed in the presence of the NL variants under the same conditions as wt Cin8.
source: Under the same conditions, MT capturing or sliding was not observed in the presence of the NL variants, consistent with the lower affinity of the NL variants for the MTs (Figure 4A) and their reduced ability to bundle MTs (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by MT sliding assay data and is consistent with MT-binding and bundling data.

claim: All the viable NL variants can reverse directionality, with more than 50% of sliding being plus-end directed.
source: Similarly to wt Cin8, in more than 50% of the cases, sliding produced by the NL variants was plus-end directed (Figure 6B), indicating that all the viable NL variants can reverse directionality.
evidence: The claim is supported by MT sliding assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The velocity of plus-end MT sliding induced by Cin8-G522N was faster than that of wt Cin8.
source: The velocity of plus-end MT sliding induced by Cin8-G522N was faster than that of wt Cin8 (Figure 6B and Figure 6—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by MT sliding assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The velocity of plus-end directed MT sliding of the Cin8NLCut7 and Cin8NLEg5-NG variants was significantly slower than that of wt Cin8.
source: Finally, the velocity of plus-end directed MT sliding of the Cin8NLCut7 and Cin8NLEg5-NG variants was significantly slower than that of wt Cin8 (Figure 6B and Figure 6—videos 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by MT sliding assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Although the NL variants can reverse to plus-end directionality during antiparallel MT sliding, their MT sliding is less efficient and requires higher motor concentrations compared to wt Cin8.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that although the NL variants can reverse to plus-end directionality during antiparallel MT sliding, their MT sliding is less efficient and requires higher motor concentrations compared to wt Cin8.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on MT sliding assay data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Mutations in the NL modulate the motile properties and intracellular functions of a bi-directional N-terminal kinesin motor.
source: The current study is the first to demonstrate that mutations in the NL modulate the motile properties and intracellular functions of a bi-directional N-terminal kinesin motor.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mutations in the NL regulate MT affinity, minus-end directed motility, and MT crosslinking and antiparallel sliding functions of the bi-directional kinesin-5, Cin8.
source: The data presented here indicates that mutations in the NL regulate MT affinity, minus-end directed motility, and MT crosslinking and antiparallel sliding functions of the bi-directional kinesin-5, Cin8.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All NL variants that can support the viability of yeast cells are able to move in the minus-end direction in vitro and localize near the SPBs prior to spindle assembly.
source: Our data demonstrates that, compared with wt Cin8, all the examined NL variants exhibited reduced affinity for MTs (Figure 4A) and an impaired ability to crosslink and slide MTs in vitro (Figure 5C–D). Importantly, our data also shows that all NL variants that can support the viability of yeast cells exhibit two common traits: (a) they are able to move in the minus-end direction in vitro (Figure 4) and (b) they localize near the SPBs prior to spindle assembly (Figure 2C–E), indicating a connection between intracellular functionality, minus-end directed motility, and localization at the SPBs.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on comparison of multiple experimental datasets (Figures 2, 4, 5).

claim: Processive minus-end directed motility that localizes the motors near the SPBs prior to spindle assembly and the subsequent reversal of directionality to produce antiparallel MT sliding are necessary for the mitotic functions of the kinesin-5 Cin8.
source: Thus, we conclude that, consistent with our model (Shapira et al., 2017; Singh et al., 2018), processive minus-end directed motility that localizes the motors near the SPBs prior to spindle assembly and the subsequent reversal of directionality to produce antiparallel MT sliding are necessary for the mitotic functions of the kinesin-5 Cin8.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on all the experimental data and is consistent with previously published models.

claim: None of the examined NL variants recapitulated the array of H-bonds formed during NL docking in wt Cin8.
source: Examination by modeling, based on known structures of four different kinesin motors in the AMP-PNP-bound state, reveals that none of the examined NL variants recapitulated the array of H-bonds formed during NL docking in wt Cin8 (Figure 3 and Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling data shown in Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: An exact H-bond array during NL docking is one of the factors required for the functioning of Cin8 NL variants.
source: All these variants are defective in intracellular functions and/or motile properties (Figures 1, 2 and 4–6), suggesting that an exact H-bond array during NL docking is one of the factors required for their functioning.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on comparison of modeling data (Figure 3 and Table 2) with experimental data (Figures 1, 2, 4-6).

claim: The overall number of H-bonds formed between the N-latch position and β10 of the NL in Cin8 is considerably smaller than that in kinesin-1 motors.
source: According to our modeling, the overall number of H-bonds formed between the N-latch position and β10 of the NL is considerably smaller than that in kinesin-1 motors (Budaitis et al., 2019; Hwang et al., 2008), suggesting decreased H-bond stabilization and increased flexibility of the docked NL of Cin8.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of modeling data with published data on kinesin-1 motors.

claim: The β7/NL H-bond stabilization is less critical for the function of Cin8 than the conserved backbone H-bond between the N-latch G522 and motor domain G157.
source: Of these stabilizing H-bond factors, the β7/NL H-bond stabilization seems to be less critical for the function of Cin8, since the Cin8NLCut7 variant that completely lacks H-bonds in this region is able to support cell viability as a sole source of kinesin-5 function, although its intracellular functionality is most defective among the NL variants examined (Figures 1 and 2 and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on comparison of modeling data (Figure 3 and Table 2) with experimental data (Figures 1 and 2 and Table 1).

claim: The conserved backbone H-bond between the N-latch G522 and the motor domain G157 is critical for Cin8 function.
source: In contrast to the β7/NL H-bond stabilization, our modeling and experimental data suggest that the conserved backbone H-bond between the N-latch G522 and the motor domain G157 is critical for Cin8 function, since its absence results in the non-functional Cin8NLCut7-NG variant (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on comparison of modeling data (Figure 3 and Table 2) with experimental data (Figure 1C).

claim: Additional stabilization of the N-latch position by H-bond formation is incompatible with the functioning of Cin8.
source: Thus, the difference between the activity of the Cin8NLEg5 and Cin8NLEg5-NG variants and the differences between their modeled H-bond configuration during NL docking suggest that additional stabilization of the N-latch position by H-bond formation is incompatible with the functioning of Cin8.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on comparison of modeling data (Figure 3 and Table 2) with experimental data (Figures 1, 2, 4-6).

claim: Certain degree of H-bond flexibility during NL docking must be maintained to enable the functioning of Cin8.
source: In other words, certain degree of H-bond flexibility during NL docking must be maintained to enable the functioning of Cin8.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on all the modeling and experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Processive stepping in the plus-end direction of kinesin-1 motors is achieved, in part, by a gating mechanism that prevents simultaneous strong binding of the two kinesin-1 motor-domain heads to MTs.
source: Recent studies indicate that processive stepping in the plus-end direction of kinesin-1 motors is achieved, in part, by a gating mechanism that prevents simultaneous strong binding of the two kinesin-1 motor-domain heads to MTs (Block, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: A different gating mechanism probably takes place during motility of plus-end directed kinesin-5 motors, which allows for simultaneous strong MT-binding of two motor domains of a dimer in a rigor state with no bound nucleotide.
source: However, a different gating mechanism probably takes place during motility of plus-end directed kinesin-5 motors (Muretta et al., 2015), which allows for simultaneous strong MT-binding of two motor domains of a dimer in a rigor state with no bound nucleotide (Chen et al., 2016; Krzysiak et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The two-headed strongly bound state of kinesin-5 motors has been attributed to the longer and more flexible NL of kinesin-5 motors.
source: The two-headed strongly bound state has been attributed to the longer and more flexible NL of kinesin-5 motors (Shastry and Hancock, 2010; Shastry and Hancock, 2011; Yildiz et al., 2008) and may be necessary for force production during antiparallel sliding of MTs in spindle assembly and elongation (Gerson-Gurwitz et al., 2009; Leary et al., 2019; Movshovich et al., 2008; Saunders and Hoyt, 1992; Sharp et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The NL dynamics of bi-directional kinesin-5 motors must be adapted for bi-directional stepping.
source: The bi-directional kinesin-5 motors have the ability to move in both plus-end and minus-end directions, in addition to their ability to crosslink and slide apart antiparallel MTs. Thus, their NL dynamics must be adapted for bi-directional stepping.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference from the bi-directional motility of these motors.

claim: Some flexibility should be maintained during NL docking of Cin8 to allow bi-directional motility.
source: Since inducing flexibility in the NL by extending the length of the NL was previously shown to enable minus-end directed back-stepping of kinesin-1 dimers (Clancy et al., 2011), we propose that some flexibility should be maintained during NL docking of Cin8 to allow bi-directional motility.
evidence: The claim is a proposal based on inference from published data and the experimental results of this study.

claim: Mutating the N-latch asparagine in the NL of kinesin-1 to alanine increased the plus-end directed motor velocity in a single-molecule motility assay.
source: That study reported that mutating the N-latch asparagine in the NL of kinesin-1 (equivalent to glycine 522 in Cin8) to alanine, which eliminates stabilizing interactions, increased the plus-end directed motor velocity in a single-molecule motility assay (Budaitis et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The velocity of all the viable Cin8 variants was significantly slower in the minus-end direction than that of wt Cin8.
source: Interestingly, we observed an opposite effect on the velocity of single-molecules of Cin8 during processive movement in the minus-end direction. The velocity of all the viable Cin8 variants was significantly slower in the minus-end direction than that of wt Cin8 (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by motility assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In all the viable Cin8 variants, the number of stabilizing H-bonds between the NL and motor domain was reduced compared to that of wt Cin8.
source: In all these variants, the number of stabilizing H-bonds between the NL and motor domain was reduced compared to that of wt Cin8 (Figure 3 and Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by modeling data shown in Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: The NL docked conformation (in the plus-end directed) is one of the intermediate conformations during active stepping of bi-directional kinesin motors.
source: Based on this difference, it is tempting to propose that the NL docked conformation (in the plus-end directed) is one of the intermediate conformations during active stepping of bi-directional kinesin motors.
evidence: The claim is a proposal based on inference from the experimental and modeling data.

claim: In the ATP-bound state the NLs of bi-directional kinesin-5 motors assume the docked conformation.
source: This notion is consistent with recent cryo-EM reports indicating that in the ATP-bound state the NLs of bi-directional kinesin-5 motors assume the docked conformation (Bell et al., 2017; Britto et al., 2016; von Loeffelholz et al., 2019), similarly to kinesin-1 motors (Sindelar et al., 2002; Sindelar and Downing, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published cryo-EM studies.

claim: In minus-end directed motility there is a dynamic equilibrium between several orientations of the NL (minus- and plus-end directed).
source: It is possible that in minus-end directed motility there is a dynamic equilibrium between several orientations of the NL (minus- and plus-end directed).
evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal based on the experimental data.

claim: Decreased stabilization of the docked NL in the plus-end direction increases the plus-end directed velocity of an exclusively plus-end directed kinesin, but may have an opposite (velocity-slowing) effect on the minus-end directed motility of the bi-directional Cin8.
source: While decreased stabilization of the docked NL in the plus-end direction increases the plus-end directed velocity of an exclusively plus-end directed kinesin (Budaitis et al., 2019), it may have an opposite (velocity-slowing) effect on the minus-end directed motility of the bi-directional Cin8.
evidence: The claim is a proposal based on comparison of the experimental data with published data.

claim: For kinesin-1, decreased stabilization of the NL reduced force production and impaired the ability of the mutant motors to transport high-load Golgi cargo vesicles.
source: For kinesin-1, decreased stabilization of the NL reduced force production and impaired the ability of the mutant motors to transport high-load Golgi cargo vesicles (Budaitis et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a published study.

claim: The intracellular functions of the bi-directional Cin8, reflected in cell viability, localization to the spindle and doubling times, were defective in cells expressing Cin8 variants with decreased H-bond stabilization of the NL.
source: Similarly, the intracellular functions of the bi-directional Cin8, reflected in cell viability, localization to the spindle and doubling times, were defective in cells expressing Cin8 variants with decreased H-bond stabilization of the NL (Figures 1–3, and Tables 1 and 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-3 and Tables 1 and 2.

claim: Each of the kinesin types is adopted to optimally perform its functions and different motility characteristics are required for optimal functioning of exclusively plus-end and bi-directional kinesins.
source: These results suggest that each of the kinesin types is adopted to optimally perform its functions and that different motility characteristics are required for optimal functioning of exclusively plus-end and bi-directional kinesins.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on comparison of the experimental data with published data on kinesin-1.

claim: The docking of the NL regulates the motor motility and intracellular functionality of bi-directional kinesin motors.
source: In summary we show here that the docking of the NL regulates the motor motility and intracellular functionality of bi-directional kinesin motors.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: For certain positions of the docked NL (such as the N-latch position), an exact H-bond stabilization is critical for function.
source: We show that for certain positions of the docked NL (such as the N-latch position), an exact H-bond stabilization is critical for function.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental and modeling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: At certain positions of the docked NL, suboptimal (too strong or too weak) NL docking stabilization is incompatible with kinesin functionality.
source: At these positions, suboptimal (too strong or too weak) NL docking stabilization is incompatible with kinesin functionality.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental and modeling data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The principle of exact H-bond stabilization at certain NL positions may be a general principle common to all bi-directional kinesin motors.
source: We believe that this may be a general principle common to all bi-directional kinesin motors (although the exact sequence of the NL can vary).
evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal based on the experimental data from Cin8.

claim: Bi-directional kinesin motors may be more sensitive to variations of H-bond stabilization at certain positions because of their ability to step in two directions.
source: Because of their ability to step in two directions, the bi-directional kinesin motors may be more sensitive to variations of H-bond stabilization at certain positions.
evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal based on the experimental data.

claim: Cin8 contains glycine at position 522 in the NL, which is conserved in kinesin-5 homologs of the Saccharomycetes class.
source: Cin8 contains glycine at position 522 in the NL, which is conserved in kinesin-5 homologs of the Saccharomycetes class (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The majority of other kinesin motors contain asparagine in the position equivalent to glycine 522 in Cin8.
source: In contrast, the majority of other kinesin motors contain asparagine in this position (Figure 1B), which is predicted to serve as a latch (N-latch), stabilizing the docked NL along the core motor domain via core H-bonds to a conserved glycine in a loop between α1 and β3 of the motor domain and to additional amino acids in β7 (Hwang et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1B and citation to published literature.

claim: Single amino acid replacements at positions where the consensus of most bi-directional kinesin-5 motors differs from the consensus of the exclusively plus-end directed kinesin-5 motors (variants Cin8-K516M, Cin8-Q520E, Cin8-M526T, and Cin8-D528K) were mostly viable.
source: We found that NL variants carrying a single amino acid replacement at positions where the consensus of most bi-directional kinesin-5 motors differs from the consensus of the exclusively plus-end directed kinesin-5 motors (variants Cin8-K516M, Cin8-Q520E, Cin8-M526T, and Cin8-D528K) were mostly viable (Figure 1C), thereby indicating these replacements do not significantly affect the functionality of Cin8 in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cin8 is a homotetrameric motor comprised of four identical subunits.
source: Since single Cin8 motors are tetramers comprised of four identical subunits (Hildebrandt et al., 2006), the maximal fluorescence intensity of a single Cin8 molecule containing four GFP molecules is expected to be ∼180 a.u.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The intensity distribution of the total Cin8-GFP population exhibited a major intensity peak containing ~65% of Cin8 particles with intensity <180 a.u.
source: The intensity distribution of the total Cin8-GFP population was consistent with this notion, in that it exhibited a major intensity peak containing ~65% of Cin8 particles with intensity <180 a.u. (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence intensity analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The maximal intensity of the major Cin8-GFP intensity peak was ~120 a.u., consistent with the average intensity of single Cin8 molecules containing one, two, three, or four fluorescent GFP molecules.
source: The maximal intensity of the peak was ~120 a.u., consistent with the average intensity of single Cin8 molecules containing one, two, three, or four fluorescent GFP molecules (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence intensity analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At least one of the two S. cerevisiae kinesin-5 motors, Cin8 and Kip1, is essential for cell viability.
source: Since at least one of the two S. cerevisiae kinesin-5 motors, Cin8 and Kip1, is essential for cell viability (Roof et al., 1992; Saunders and Hoyt, 1992), the NL variants were examined on a low-copy centromeric plasmid in cells carrying chromosomal deletions of CIN8 and KIP1, following the shuffling-out of the Cin8 plasmid that covered the double deletion (Figure 1C; Avunie-Masala et al., 2011; Goldstein et al., 2019; Goldstein et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The non-motor N-terminus of the plus-end directed kinesin-5 Eg5 forms a β-sheet cover strand bundle (CSB) with β9 of the docked NL, which stabilizes the docked NL configuration.
source: In this context, we note that it has previously been suggested that the non-motor N-terminus of the plus-end directed kinesin-5 Eg5 forms a β-sheet cover strand bundle (CSB) with β9 of the docked NL, which stabilizes the docked NL configuration (Goulet et al., 2012; Goulet et al., 2014), similarly to reports for kinesin-1 motors (Hwang et al., 2008; Khalil et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: A recent cryo-EM study of MT-bound S. pombe Cut7 indicates that a similar CSB formation may also take place during NL docking in bi-directional kinesin-5 motors.
source: A recent cryo-EM study of MT-bound S. pombe Cut7 indicates that a similar CSB formation may also take place during NL docking in bi-directional kinesin-5 motors (von Loeffelholz et al., 2019), despite the fact that the non-motor N-terminal region is considerably longer in bi-directional kinesin-5 motors compared to exclusively plus-end directed kinesin-5 and kinesin-1 motors (Singh et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: CSB formation stabilizes NL docking in Cin8 and may affect NL dynamics.
source: Thus, it is likely that CSB formation stabilizes NL docking in Cin8 and may affect NL dynamics.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from published literature and the modeling data.

claim: The differences in H-bond formation between β9 and the motor domain, as depicted by modeling, cannot explain the differences in functionality between the NL variants of Cin8.
source: Thus, we conclude that the differences in H-bond formation between β9 and the motor domain, as depicted by our modeling, cannot explain the differences in functionality between the NL variants of Cin8.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on comparison of modeling data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) with experimental data (Figure 1C).

claim: The significantly reduced intracellular functionality of the Cin8NLCut7 variant can be explained, at least in part, by combination of its defective motor functions.
source: Thus, the significantly reduced intracellular functionality of the Cin8NLCut7 variant (Figure 1C) can be explained, at least in part, by combination of its defective motor functions, such as reduced MT binding (Figure 4A), reduced velocity (Figure 4D) and processivity (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) on the single-molecule level and reduced efficiency of crosslinking and sliding apart antiparallel MTs (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on comparison of multiple experimental datasets.

claim: The ability to produce processive minus-end directed motility is one of the motility traits that are important for the intracellular functioning of Cin8.
source: Thus, our results suggest that that the ability to produce processive minus-end directed motility is one of the motility traits that are important for the intracellular functioning of Cin8.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on comparison of motility data (Figure 4) with viability data (Figure 1C).

claim: The intracellular functions of kinesin-5 motors are attributed to their ability to crosslink the interpolar MTs of the spindle.
source: The intracellular functions of kinesin-5 motors are attributed to their ability to crosslink the interpolar MTs of the spindle (Goulet and Moores, 2013; Mann and Wadsworth, 2019; Singh et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: One of the factors that affects the directionality and velocity of Cin8 is its accumulation in clusters on MTs.
source: We have previously demonstrated that one of the factors that affects the directionality and velocity of Cin8 is its accumulation in clusters on MTs (Shapira et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previously published study.

claim: Cin8 can reverse directionality from minus- to plus-end directed motility due to forces opposing the directional motility, which are referred to as drag.
source: We have recently suggested that Cin8 can reverse directionality from minus- to plus-end directed motility due to forces opposing the directional motility, which we referred to as drag (Pandey et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a recently published study.

claim: In the absence of a considerable applied drag force, MT sliding can also be minus-end directed, similarly to the single molecule motility under the high salt conditions.
source: In accordance with this notion, in the absence of a considerable applied drag force, MT sliding can also be minus-end directed, similarly to the single molecule motility under the high salt conditions (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: The bi-directional and minus-end directed MT sliding observed results from a low local concentration of Cin8 motors in the overlapping MT region and/or reduced MT affinity of the NL variants.
source: Based on this model, we propose that the bi-directional and minus-end directed MT sliding we observed here results from a low local concentration of Cin8 motors in the overlapping MT region and/or reduced MT affinity of the NL variants (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is a proposal based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: If sufficient motors are present locally between overlapping MT of the spindle, antiparallel plus-end directed MT sliding can take place to produce an outwardly directed force that separates the SPBs apart.
source: However, the fact that all the examined Cin8 motors can produce plus-end directed MT sliding suggests that if sufficient motors are present locally between overlapping MT of the spindle, antiparallel plus-end directed MT sliding can take place to produce an outwardly directed force that separates the SPBs apart.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on inference from the MT sliding data (Figure 6).

claim: For fungal kinesin-5 motors to perform their spindle assembly function in closed mitosis, they need first to localize near the SPBs by their minus-end directed motility and then to reverse directionality to plus-end directed motility between antiparallel MTs in order to produce antiparallel MT sliding and separate the SPBs apart.
source: We have previously suggested that for fungal kinesin-5 motors to perform their spindle assembly function in closed mitosis, they need first to localize near the SPBs by their minus-end directed motility and then to reverse directionality to plus-end directed motility between antiparallel MTs in order to produce antiparallel MT sliding and separate the SPBs apart (Shapira et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previously published study.

claim: Decreasing the number of stabilizing H-bonds resulted in partially functional variants, as long as a conserved backbone H-bond at the N-latch position remained intact.
source: Decreasing the number of stabilizing H-bonds resulted in partially functional variants, as long as a conserved backbone H-bond at the N-latch position (proposed to stabilize the docked conformation of the NL) remained intact.
evidence: The claim is a summary of findings from the Abstract, supported by experimental and modeling data.

claim: Elimination of the conserved backbone H-bond at the N-latch position resulted in production of a non-functional Cin8 variant.
source: Elimination of this conserved H-bond resulted in production of a non-functional Cin8 variant.
evidence: The claim is a summary of findings from the Abstract, supported by experimental data.

claim: Additional H-bond stabilization of the N-latch position, generated by replacement of the NL of Cin8 by sequences of the plus-end directed kinesin-5 Eg5, produced a nonfunctional variant.
source: Surprisingly, additional H-bond stabilization of the N-latch position, generated by replacement of the NL of Cin8 by sequences of the plus-end directed kinesin-5 Eg5, also produced a nonfunctional variant.
evidence: The claim is a summary of findings from the Abstract, supported by experimental and modeling data.

claim: In the Cin8NLEg5 variant, a single replacement of N-latch asparagine with glycine eliminated the additional H-bond stabilization and rescued the functional defects.
source: In that variant, a single replacement of N-latch asparagine with glycine, as present in Cin8, eliminated the additional H-bond stabilization and rescued the functional defects.
evidence: The claim is a summary of findings from the Abstract, supported by experimental and modeling data.

claim: Exact N-latch stabilization during NL docking is critical for the function of bi-directional kinesin-5 Cin8.
source: We conclude that exact N-latch stabilization during NL docking is critical for the function of bi-directional kinesin-5 Cin8.
evidence: The claim is the main conclusion from the Abstract, supported by all experimental and modeling data.
